scenes.title: Measure error, move lens, snap sharp

vo.text: You tap to focus, and a blurry scene snaps sharp in a fraction of a second.
Early cameras had to hunt back and forth to guess the right lens position.
Modern autofocus creates two copies of the same subject from opposite sides of the lens.
When the subject is out of focus, those copies are separated. When focused, they align.
The camera measures that separation to know exactly how far and which direction to move the lens.
A focus motor then drives the lens directly to the calculated position.
Contrast detection then makes a final tiny adjustment for peak sharpness.
So split images tell the camera where to go, and the lens moves straight to sharp focus.
